newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen rebel gives up politics for computers.
newsitem.headline: Chechen rebel gives up politics for computers.

text.p: Chechen rebel Shamil Basayev, Russia's most wanted "terrorist", conceded defeat on Wednesday in the separatist region's presidential election and said he would quit politics for the computer business.
Preliminary results showed senior guerrilla commander Aslan Maskhadov won with 64.8 percent to Basayev's 22.7 percent and 10.2 percent for acting separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev.

The black-bearded Basayev, 32, made his name by leading a bloody hostage-taking raid against the Russian town of Budennovsk in June 1995. From his base in the southern mountains he was one of the Chechens' most successful guerrilla leaders.

Swapping his Kalashnikov and combat fatigues for a smart city coat and hat, he campaigned energetically for Monday's post-war election, accusing Maskhadov, the guerrillas' overall commander, of surrounding himself with "criminals".
Basayev's strong language raised fears of a schism in the ranks of the heavily armed rebels that might lead to civil war. But on Wednesday he made clear he would not oppose Maskhadov.
"I won't get in his way, that's the main thing," Basayev told reporters at his campaign headquarters in the devastated Minutka district of the Chechen capital Grozny.
He added that if Maskhadov ditched some of his aides he would work for him "even as a janitor".
"Once a majority of the people have given him their confidence to govern, I won't bother him. I will get on with my own private life," Basayev said.
"I will get on with business, the computer business," he added. Some of Basayev's entourage were among a group which first brought an Internet service to Grozny.
"We'll get on well," Basayev said of Maskhadov. "He was our leader in this war, so I don't have any problem with that."
Basayev said he did not see his political career as a failure and put his defeat down to a lack of campaign financing.
"I'm in a good mood and don't consider I've lost. I haven't lost in any way, you could say we just did not succeed."
Despite his failure to win the presidency, Basayev is widely admired in Chechnya for his bold conduct during the 21-month war against Russia and for his direct style of speaking.

During the election campaign he called for a vigorous crackdown on crime in the tiny mountainous region and accused his opponents, including Maskhadov, of allowing pro-Moscow officials to regain positions of influence.
